STEPPARENT ADOPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan A. Rivera · Taylor M. Rivera

DECLARATION OF PURPOSE — STEPPARENT ADOPTION INFORMATION SHEET
This Stepparent Adoption — Information Sheet describes California's statutory process for Jordan A. Rivera, the spouse or domestic partner of Taylor M. Rivera, to adopt Taylor M. Rivera's child, Sam T. Rivera (born June 12, 2016), under California Family Code Division 13, Part 2, Chapter 5 (Stepparent Adoptions, §§ 9000–9007). It is prepared for use alongside an actual stepparent adoption petition contemplated for filing in the California superior court for Sacramento County.

A stepparent adoption is its own distinct statutory track — separate from an independent adoption by a non-relative and from an agency adoption — and it is legally distinct from a guardianship of a minor's person. A guardianship, addressed by this corpus's separate Guardianship of the Person (Petition Information Sheet) document, gives a court-appointed guardian custody, care, and control of a child without terminating any parent's legal rights and without creating a new legal parent. A completed adoption is different in both respects: it creates a new legal parent-child relationship between Sam T. Rivera and Jordan A. Rivera, and it ends the parental rights of any parent whose rights are not preserved by law or by an executed waiver.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not adopt Sam T. Rivera, does not terminate any parent's rights, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only a final court decree of adoption, entered after the statutory petition, consent, investigation, and hearing process described in this document's companion clauses, can actually do that.

WHO MAY FILE A STEPPARENT ADOPTION PETITION, AND THE STATUTORY CHAPTER IT FALLS UNDER
California law authorizes an unmarried minor to be adopted by an adult under Family Code Part 2. Within that part, a separate chapter — Chapter 5, "Stepparent Adoptions," Family Code §§ 9000–9007 — governs the specific case of Jordan A. Rivera adopting Taylor M. Rivera's child, Sam T. Rivera. Family Code § 9000(a) authorizes "a stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent’s spouse" to "file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5," and § 9000(b) extends the same filing right to "a domestic partner, as defined in Section 297, desiring to adopt a child of the other domestic partner." California generally requires a prospective adoptive parent to be at least 10 years older than the child being adopted, but Family Code § 8601(b) lets a court dispense with that age-gap requirement specifically for a stepparent (or certain other close relatives) where the court is satisfied the adoption "is in the best interest of the parties and is in the public interest."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An unmarried minor may be adopted by an adult as provided in this part."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8600 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8600 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8600.)
  "A stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent’s spouse may for that purpose file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.)
  "A domestic partner, as defined in Section 297, desiring to adopt a child of the other domestic partner may, for that purpose, file a petition in any county authorized pursuant to Section 8609.5."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.)
  "If the court is satisfied that the adoption of a child by a stepparent, or by a sister, brother, aunt, uncle, or first cousin and, if that person is married, by that person and that person’s spouse, is in the best interest of the parties and is in the public interest, it may approve the adoption without regard to the ages of the child and the prospective adoptive parent or parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8601(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8601(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8601.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may file a stepparent adoption petition in California and of the statutory chapter that governs it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption; who may file, and under what chapter, vary by state. Two of these citations, § 9000(a) and § 9000(b), are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 9000); § 8601(b) and § 8600 are separate, independently cited sections. This clause corrects an imprecise assumption in the original research brief, which described stepparent adoption as falling "under the independent adoption framework" and referenced a section range of "§§ 8900-8823" (a backward, non-existent range). On the verified statutory text, stepparent adoption is its own separate chapter (Chapter 5, §§ 9000–9007) within Family Code Part 2 ("Adoption of Unmarried Minors," §§ 8600–9212); it is not part of the independent-adoption chapter, and § 8900 is instead the starting section of a different chapter altogether — intercountry adoptions — as confirmed by this document's companion clause on the legal effect of adoption, which cites § 8617(c)'s own cross-reference to "intercountry adoptions governed by Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 8900)." This document does not further detail the separate independent-adoption or agency-adoption chapters, or the venue rules in § 8609.5 that § 9000(a) and (b) cross-reference, beyond confirming that a filing county must be one § 8609.5 authorizes. This document is informational only: it does not itself file a petition, and it does not determine that the petitioner named in this document is eligible to adopt the child named in this document in any specific case.

THE INVESTIGATIVE REPORT REQUIRED BEFORE THE COURT RULES, AND ITS COST
Before granting or denying Jordan A. Rivera's request to adopt Sam T. Rivera, Family Code § 9001(a) requires the court to "review and consider a written investigative report," though that report "shall not require a home study unless so ordered by the court upon request of an investigator or interested person, or on the court’s own motion." The investigator may be a probation officer, a qualified court investigator, the county welfare department, or — if the petitioner elects and pays the investigator directly — a licensed clinical social worker, licensed marriage and family therapist, licensed professional clinical counselor, or private licensed adoption agency. Family Code § 9002 makes the prospective adoptive parent liable for the reasonable costs of that investigation, capped at "a maximum of seven hundred dollars ($700)," and lets the investigating office "defer, waive, or reduce the fee if its payment would cause economic hardship to the prospective adoptive parent detrimental to the welfare of the adopted child."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  "The report in a stepparent adoption case shall not require a home study unless so ordered by the court upon request of an investigator or interested person, or on the court’s own motion."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9001(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9001(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9001.)
  "in a stepparent adoption, the prospective adoptive parent is liable for all reasonable costs incurred in connection with the stepparent adoption, including, but not limited to, costs incurred for the investigation required by Section 9001, up to a maximum of seven hundred dollars ($700)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9002 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9002 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9002.)
  "The court, probation officer, qualified court investigator, or county welfare department may defer, waive, or reduce the fee if its payment would cause economic hardship to the prospective adoptive parent detrimental to the welfare of the adopted child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9002 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9002 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9002.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the pre-decision investigation requirement and its cost in a California stepparent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what investigation, if any, another state's process requires. § 9001 and § 9002 are two different statutory sections, cited independently rather than as subsections of one section; only subdivision (a) of § 9001 is quoted here, and this clause does not detail § 9001(b)'s and (c)'s further procedural rules for who conducts the investigation, or § 9001(d)'s confirmation that this section does not require the State Department of Social Services to issue regulations for stepparent adoptions. Both sections open with the phrase "Except as provided in Section 9000.5": a separate statutory exception, detailed in this document's companion clause, removes this investigation-and-fee requirement entirely for a narrower category of stepparent adoptions. This document is informational only: it does not itself investigate, report on, or determine the suitability of the petitioner named in this document or the home in which the child named in this document resides, and it does not determine whether an investigation will be required, waived, or reduced in any specific case.

A NARROWER STATUTORY EXCEPTION: NO DEFAULT INVESTIGATION, FEE, MINIMUM MARRIAGE DURATION, OR HEARING
A separate, narrower procedure in Family Code § 9000.5 applies where the child was born during the marriage or domestic partnership and either the parent being adopted from gave birth to the child, or the child was born through gestational surrogacy and only one spouse's or partner's parentage was established under the Uniform Parentage Act or a related parentage proceeding. For a stepparent adoption that meets that description, § 9000.5(b)(1) provides that, "unless otherwise ordered by the court for good cause," the adoption does not require "a home investigation pursuant to Section 9001 or a home study," the costs described in Section 9002, or "a hearing pursuant to Section 9007." Section 9000.5(b)(2) further provides that the parties "shall not be required to have been married or in a domestic partnership ... for a minimum period of time prior to the adoption being granted or to provide verification of their income or education." The court grants the adoption under this section upon finding, per § 9000.5(e), that the parties were married or partnered at the time of the child's birth and that any other person with a claim to the child's parentage who must be given notice of, or consent to, the adoption has been noticed or has consented.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The procedures provided in this section apply to a stepparent adoption where the child was born during the marriage or domestic partnership, including a registered domestic partnership or civil union from another jurisdiction, and either of the following circumstances applies: (1) One of the spouses or partners gave birth to the child. (2) The child was born through a gestational surrogacy process brought about by one or both of the spouses or partners, and the parentage of only one spouse or partner was established pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12) or another parentage proceeding related to the surrogacy."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.5.)

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000.5(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.5.)
  "In stepparent adoptions under this section, the parties shall not be required to have been married or in a domestic partnership, including a registered domestic partnership or civil union from another jurisdiction, for a minimum period of time prior to the adoption being granted or to provide verification of their income or education."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000.5(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000.5(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.5.)
  "The court shall grant the stepparent adoption under this section upon finding both of the following: (1) That the parent who gave birth, or who caused the birth through gestational surrogacy, and the spouse or partner who is adopting were married or in a domestic partnership, including a registered domestic partnership or civil union from another jurisdiction, at the time of the child’s birth. (2) Any other person with a claim to parentage of the child who is required to be provided notice of, or who must consent to, the adoption has been noticed or provided consent to the adoption."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9000.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9000.5(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9000.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a narrower, procedurally lighter path available for some California stepparent adoptions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, and not a claim that the proposed adoption of the child named in this document by the petitioner named in this document qualifies for this narrower path; whether it does depends on the specific facts of the child's birth and parentage. All four citations in this clause — § 9000.5(a), § 9000.5(b)(1), § 9000.5(b)(2), and § 9000.5(e) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 9000.5); they are treated here as one source, not four independent ones. This exception does not dispense with any required notice to, or consent from, a person with a claim to the child's parentage — § 9000.5(d)-(e) instead condition the grant of the adoption on that notice or consent having already been given, and § 9000.5(c)'s filing requirements (a marriage or partnership certificate, the child's birth certificate, and parentage declarations) are not otherwise detailed in this clause. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that this narrower procedure applies to any specific adoption, and it does not grant, or purport to grant, any adoption.

WHOSE CONSENT IS GENERALLY REQUIRED FROM THE CHILD'S OTHER PARENT
California's general adoption-consent statutes, applicable to a stepparent adoption of Sam T. Rivera along with the rest of Family Code Part 2, turn on whether the child has a presumed father under Family Code § 7611. Family Code § 8604(a) provides that, subject to a stated exception, "a child having a presumed father under Section 7611 shall not be adopted without the consent of the child’s birth parents, if living." Where the child has no presumed father, only one parent's consent is required: Family Code § 8605 provides that "a child not having a presumed father under Section 7611 may not be adopted without the consent of the child’s mother, if living." For a stepparent adoption specifically, Family Code § 9003(a) further requires that "the consent of either or both birth parents shall be signed in the presence of a notary public, court clerk, probation officer, qualified court investigator, authorized representative of a licensed adoption agency, or county welfare department staff member of any county of this state," and that the person before whom it is signed "shall immediately file the consent with the clerk of the court where the adoption request is filed."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8605 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8605 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8605.)

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9003(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9003(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9003.)
  "The petitioner, petitioner’s counsel, or person before whom the consent is signed shall immediately file the consent with the clerk of the court where the adoption request is filed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9003(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9003(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9003.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's general consent framework for an adoption of a minor, including a stepparent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, and not a claim about whose consent is or is not required for the specific adoption of the child named in this document, which depends on facts such as whether that child has a presumed father under § 7611. The three citations in this clause are three separate statutory sections — § 8604(a), § 8605, and § 9003(a) — none a subsection of another; they are not treated as a single source. This clause does not detail § 7611's own presumed-father standards, or § 8604(a)'s further proviso limiting when a presumed father's consent is required based on the timing of the mother's relinquishment or termination of her rights. The circumstances in which a required parent's consent may instead be dispensed with, and the separate requirement that a child over 12 consent to their own adoption, are addressed in this document's companion clauses. This document is informational only: it does not itself obtain, record, or determine the necessity of any parent's consent to the adoption of the child named in this document.

THE STATUTORY CATEGORIES IN WHICH A PARENT'S CONSENT MAY BE DISPENSED WITH, AND THE EFFECT OF A REFUSAL
California law identifies specific, defined categories in which a required parent's consent to an adoption is dispensed with, rather than leaving that determination to case-by-case discretion untethered to any standard. Family Code § 8604(b) allows the parent who has sole custody, by judicial order or agreement, to consent alone where "the other birth parent for a period of one year willfully fails to communicate with, and to pay for, the care, support, and education of the child when able to do so," but only after that other parent "has been served with a copy of a citation ... that requires the birth parent not having custody to appear" in court. Section 8604(c) provides that failure to support or communicate for that one-year period "is prima facie evidence that the failure was willful and without lawful excuse," while "token efforts to support or communicate" may be disregarded by the court. Separately, Family Code § 8606 lists categories in which a birth parent's consent is not necessary at all, including where the parent "has been judicially deprived of the custody and control of the child" by a court order freeing the child from that parent's custody and control under Family Code Part 4 (commencing with § 7800) or a comparable Welfare and Institutions Code order, or where the parent "has deserted the child without provision for identification of the child." Within the stepparent-adoption chapter itself, Family Code § 9006(b) states the converse consequence when none of these categories applies and consent is not obtained: "If a birth parent has refused to give the required consent, the adoption petition shall be dismissed."

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8604(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8604(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8604.)

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8604(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8604(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8604.)

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8606(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8606(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8606.)
  "Where the birth parent has deserted the child without provision for identification of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8606(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8606(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8606.)
  "If a birth parent has refused to give the required consent, the adoption petition shall be dismissed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9006(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9006(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9006.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the defined statutory categories under which California law dispenses with a parent's consent to an adoption, and of what happens under the stepparent-adoption chapter when a required consent is refused — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption. Two of these citations, § 8604(b) and § 8604(c), are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source; two others, § 8606(a) and § 8606(c), are likewise subsections of one section (§ 8606) and are treated as a second, separate source; § 9006(b) is a third, independently cited section. Section 8606 lists additional categories not quoted or detailed here — subdivisions (b), (d), and (e), covering a voluntary surrender in another jurisdiction and a relinquishment for adoption. This clause does not further detail the freedom-from-parental-custody-and-control proceeding under Family Code Part 4 (§ 7800 et seq.) that § 8606(a) cross-references; that is a separate court proceeding with its own petition, findings, and standard of proof, which this document does not describe. Most importantly: this clause states the categories the statute defines; it does not state, and should not be read as stating, that the other parent identified in this document — or any specific parent — has willfully failed to communicate with or support the child named in this document, has made only token efforts to do so, has deserted that child, or has otherwise had their consent dispensed with by law. Whether any of these categories applies to a specific parent in a specific case is a factual and legal determination for a court to make on the evidence presented, and this information sheet does not make, and does not purport to make, that determination. This document is informational only: it does not itself dispense with any parent's consent, and it does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted.

THE CHILD'S OWN CONSENT TO THE ADOPTION
Separate from any parent's consent, California law requires the child's own consent above a stated age. Family Code § 8602 provides in full: "The consent of a child, if over the age of 12 years, is necessary to the child’s adoption."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The consent of a child, if over the age of 12 years, is necessary to the child’s adoption."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 8602 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 8602 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=8602.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law requires a child's own consent to an adoption above a stated age — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about whether the child named in this document's own consent is or is not required. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 8602); no additional independent source was found for this. The statute's own wording is "if over the age of 12 years" — worded differently from the "12 years of age or older" phrasing this corpus's companion Guardianship of the Person (Petition Information Sheet) document quotes from a different code section (Probate Code § 1510(a)) governing a different proceeding. This clause reports only § 8602's own words and takes no position on, and did not independently verify, how courts or secondary sources construe "over the age of 12" as applied to a child who has just turned 12. This document is informational only: it does not itself obtain or record the consent of the child named in this document, and does not determine whether that consent is required in this specific case.

THE LEGAL EFFECT OF A COMPLETED STEPPARENT ADOPTION
Once an adoption is completed, Family Code § 8616 provides that "the adopted child and the adoptive parents shall sustain towards each other the legal relationship of parent and child and have all the rights and are subject to all the duties of that relationship" — meaning Jordan A. Rivera would become Sam T. Rivera's legal parent for all purposes, not merely a stepparent. As to any parent whose rights are not preserved, Family Code § 8617(a) provides that, subject to one exception, "the existing parent or parents of an adopted child are, from the time of the adoption, relieved of all parental duties towards, and all responsibility for, the adopted child, and have no right over the child." That termination "may be waived if both the existing parent or parents and the prospective adoptive parent or parents sign a waiver at any time prior to the finalization of the adoption," per § 8617(b), and § 8617(c) confirms this framework "applies to all adoptions except intercountry adoptions governed by Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 8900)." Stepparent adoptions carry one further, statutorily required notice that distinguishes them from many other adoptions on this specific point: Family Code § 9004 requires the consent form given to a birth parent to state, in substance, "If you and your child lived together at any time as parent and child, the adoption of your child through a stepparent adoption does not affect the child’s right to inherit your property or the property of other blood relatives."

  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the legal effect a completed adoption has under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, and not a claim that any specific adoption of the child named in this document has been, or will be, completed. Three of these citations — § 8617(a), § 8617(b), and § 8617(c) — are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source; § 8616 and § 9004 are separate, independently cited sections. This clause does not detail Probate Code inheritance rules beyond the specific notice text Family Code § 9004 itself requires; it reports that required notice as a Family Code provision, not as independent verification of Probate Code text. As stated in this document's declaration clause, and confirmed here, this legal effect is what distinguishes a completed adoption from a guardianship of a minor's person: a guardianship does not relieve any parent of parental duties or rights under § 8617, and does not create the parent-child relationship § 8616 describes. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any parent-child relationship, does not terminate any parent's rights, and does not determine that any specific adoption of the child named in this document is or should be granted. Only a final court decree of adoption produces the legal effects described in this clause.

INFORMATION REFERENCED WHEN A STEPPARENT ADOPTION PETITION IS FILED
For reference: Jordan A. Rivera is identified as the stepparent or domestic partner proposing to adopt Sam T. Rivera, born June 12, 2016, the child of Jordan A. A stepparent adoption is its own distinct statutory track — separate from an independent adoption by a non-relative and from an agency adoption — and it is legally distinct from a guardianship of a minor's person. A guardianship, addressed by this corpus's separate Guardianship of the Person (Petition Information Sheet) document, gives a court-appointed guardian custody, care, and control of a child without terminating any parent's legal rights and without creating a new legal parent. California law authorizes an unmarried minor to be adopted by an adult under Family Code Part 2. Within that part, a separate chapter — Chapter 5, "Stepparent Adoptions," Family Code §§ 9000–9007 — governs the specific case of Jordan A. Rivera adopting Taylor M. Rivera's child, Sam T. Rivera. expectedJSON.body: California law identifies specific, defined categories in which a required parent's consent to an adoption is dispensed with, rather than leaving that determination to case-by-case discretion untethered to any standard. Family Code § 8604(b) allows the parent who has sole custody, by judicial order or agreement, to consent alone where "the other birth parent for a period of one year willfully fails to communicate with, and to pay for, the care, support, and education of the child when able to do so," but only after that other parent "has been served with a copy of a citation ... that requires the birth parent not having custody to appear" in court. Section 8604(c) provides that failure to support or communicate for that one-year period "is prima facie evidence that the failure was willful and without lawful excuse," while "token efforts to support or communicate" may be disregarded by the court. Separately, Family Code § 8606 lists categories in which a birth parent's consent is not necessary at all, including where the parent "has been judicially deprived of the custody and control of the child" by a court order freeing the child from that parent's custody and control under Family Code Part 4 (commencing with § 7800) or a comparable Welfare and Institutions Code order, or where the parent "has deserted the child without provision for identification of the child." Within the stepparent-adoption chapter itself, Family Code § 9006(b) states the converse consequence when none of these categories applies and consent is not obtained: "If a birth parent has refused to give the required consent, the adoption petition shall be dismissed."
